title: TB8-03529
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria, appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated November 29, 2017, rejecting her claim for refugee protection.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The Appellant's allegations are set out in her Basis of Claim (BOC) form.1 In summary, she fears her father and XXXX XXXX XXXX(the Chief), as her father promised that she would marry the Chief when he could not repay a loan. Additionally, she fears her boyfriend because, after becoming pregnant with his child, he insisted that she undergo female genital mutilation (FGM).

She alleges that she obtained a visa to the United States of America (USA) on XXXX XXXX, 2016. On XXXX XXXX, 2017 she left Nigeria for Turkey where she remained until XXXX of 2017. On XXXX XXXX, 2017 she left Nigeria for the USA. On XXXX XXXX, 2017 she entered Canada and made an inland refugee claim on July 13, 2017.

The Appellant has submitted a report from a psychotherapist dated XXXX XXXX, 2018. Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim, or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the hearing. If the proposed new evidence does meet the requirements of subsection 110(4), I must then apply the analysis set out in the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Raza2 as subsequently modified by the same court's decision in Singh.3

While the report is dated after the RPD decision, it was reasonably available to be presented at the time of the RPD hearing, as the report is based on the Appellant's mental state as a result of the alleged incidents in Nigeria. Further, as there were multiple hearing dates the Appellant, who was represented by counsel, could have obtained a psychological report after either of the first two hearings, if the nature of the hearing caused her distress such that special consideration was required when assessing her credibility. As such, I do not accept this report as new evidence.
As no new evidence was accepted, I will not hold a hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

While reviewing the RPD decision, I am required to independently determine whether the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of law, fact or mixed fact and law. I may defer to the RPD's credibility assessment of oral testimony if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage in the circumstances.4 Reasons will be provided in my analysis if I find that the RPD had a meaningful advantage.5 ANALYSIS

I have conducted an independent assessment of the evidence, the testimony before the RPD, the RPD decision, as well as the Appellant's submissions, and find that the RPD did not err in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility for the reasons discussed below. Application of the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution

When assessing the Appellant's credibility, the RPD took the following factors into consideration: that she is an educated women, 32 years old, who has completed the coursework for a degree in XXXX XXXX XXXX, who undertook a XXXXapprenticeship, who did not present as simpleminded nor unsophisticated, who traveled independently to the USA, found shelter, then made her way to Canada where she again found shelter and retained counsel. The RPD also considered that the Appellant displayed obvious anxiety at each hearing, and by the final hearing was quite late in her pregnancy. I will assess this case with the same factors in mind.

When assessing this case, the RPD used the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution,6 specifically with respect to forced marriage and FGM, to guide its reasoning. I will do the same. Inconsistencies and omissions

The RPD found that the Appellant was not a credible witness who did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the events outlined in her BOC occurred. The RPD further found that the Appellant's inconsistencies and omissions in her testimony, when compared to her written evidence, were enough to rebut the presumption that sworn testimony is true.7 The Appellant argues that the panel displayed an unreasonable zeal to find fault in the Appellant's case even where none exists.

I agree with the RPD and find that the Appellant did not have reasonable explanations when confronted with inconsistences and omissions. I further find that the Appellant's testimonial failings cannot be attributed to her physical state, her psychological state, or other hearing room factors. I did not find that the RPD was over-vigilant nor microscopic in its examination of the evidence. My reasons for these findings are below. The claim regarding the Chief

The Appellant alleges that the RPD erred by failing to accept the Appellant's explanation for her omission in her BOC regarding the Chief looking for her at her boyfriend's house and at school, and her changing responses when this omission was put to her. The RPD noted that when these omissions where put to her, the Appellant first replied that when she wrote the BOC she was not settled in her mind, and then later changed her response to say that she did not write everything as her story would be too long.

I have listened to the hearing and I note that the Appellant gave three responses to why she did not include the story of the Chief trying to find her at her boyfriend's house and at school in her BOC. A first she says that she was not sure if she should write it, then she said she could not remember everything at the time of writing the BOC because her mind was not settled, then she says that she thought it was too much to write and that it would be too long.8 These answers are not consistent. As the Appellant's fear of the Chief goes to the heart of her claim, I find that the omission, and the subsequent inconsistency in the reasons given for the omission, undermines the Appellant's credibility.

The Appellant alleges that the RPD erred by making a negative credibility finding due to the inconsistency between the Appellant's testimony and the affidavit from her sister. The Appellant explains that this was an error because the RPD's reasons were unclear and because the RPD ventured into microscopic and irrelevant considerations. The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony that her sister did not remember how many times she called the Appellant to tell her about the Chief attempting to find her, was unreasonable and further, found that there is an inconsistency in the Appellant's own internal evidence.

At the first hearing on September 6, 2017, the Appellant stated that from February to June of 2017 she spoke with her sister on the phone about once a week and that her sister recounted to her that the Chief came in XXXX and XXXX all the time, XXXX more than three times, and that in XXXX her sister went outside to call her because the Chief was in their house.9 When the RPD put to the Appellant that the sister's affidavit, which is dated as signed in August of 2017, says that she called the Appellant twice to tell her that the Chief had been coming to the house, the Appellant replied that her sister had written that she called the Appellant twice in June. In her affidavit, the Appellant's sister states that she has not seen her sister since December 2016, but they have spoken on the phone, and specifically states that she has called the Appellant on two occasions to tell her how the Chief has been coming to their house and how their father was beaten into a coma.10

I find that the Appellant's testimony was internally inconsistent, and that it was inconsistent with her sister's affidavit. I agree with the RPD that these inconsistencies further undermine the Appellant's credibility. Further, as the basis of one half of her claim is that she fears a Chief who is pursuing her, and as the Appellant's own testimony conflicts with her sister's affidavit regarding facts that go to her heart of her claim, I assign the sister's affidavit no weight.

The Appellant alleges that the RPD did not put to her the inconsistency of her testimony regarding the incident where the Chief's boys almost caught her on campus. This is factually untrue, as this inconsistency was put to the Appellant twice directly during the hearing.11 The Appellant replied by stating that it was just a movement she noticed that made her go to security.12 I find that this explanation does not alleviate the credibility concerns laid out by the RPD, and I find that, on a balance of probabilities, this story about the men almost finding her on campus was added to embellish her claim. As this goes to the heart of her claim, I find that this further undermines her credibility.

Due to the inconsistencies, omissions and embellishments, I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that she is being sought by the Chief for forced marriage. The claim regarding the Appellant's baby's father

The Appellant alleges that the RPD had no adequate reason to render the email from the Appellant's boyfriend weightless. The RPD took adverse inference from the Appellant's failure to mention in her testimony that her boyfriend was a member of a fraternity, as well as her inability to give a reason for the omission.13 I agree that this is a material omission in both the Appellant's BOC and in her testimony, as this was listed in the email as a main reason why the Appellant should be afraid of her boyfriend. On a balance of probabilities, I find that this email was provided to embellish her claim.

Due to this omission and embellishment, I find that the Appellant has not established that her baby's father is looking for the Appellant to force her, or her baby, to undergo FGM. Delay in leaving and re-availment

The Appellant alleges that the RPD failed to consider the personal circumstances surrounding the Appellant's departure. The RPD found that the Appellant's reasons for delay were not reasonable and not internally consistent. The RPD further found the Appellant's reason for re-availment inconsistent with her BOC.

While I note that the Appellant's assertions regarding gender inequality in Nigeria are consistent with the country documents,14 it is the Appellant's inconsistencies that undermine her claim. As the RPD notes, it is not reasonable that the Appellant's boyfriend come up with the idea that the Appellant should flee the country due to her extreme fear of the Chief, then assist her in obtaining a visa, and then instead of helping her to leave the country, wait several months before taking her on all-expenses paid trip to Turkey. The Appellant cannot rely on her flight from her country as evidence of her fear, when she did not leave her country because of the Chief at any time. Even by her own evidence, she left for Turkey, then returned to Nigeria, and then left Nigeria because of an event with her boyfriend, not the Chief. Remaining Evidence

The Appellant alleges that the RPD did not properly assess the remaining evidence, specifically the affidavits from the Appellant's friend, XXXX XXXX, and from her sister, on their merits. The RPD found that given that the Appellant's allegations regarding forced marriage and FGM are not credible, the affidavit from her friend was submitted to bolster her claim. The RPD assessed the affidavit from her sister in the section regarding the claim against the Chief, as have I, and as such I will not repeat the assessment here.

The affidavit from XXXX XXXX lists only information that she has been told by the Appellant or by the Appellant's sister.15 Ms XXXX does not assert that she was a direct witness to any visits from the Chief or anyone employed by him, or was present for any conversations with the Appellant and her boyfriend. As such, this affidavit cannot overcome the credibility concerns listed above, and cannot be given any weight.

For the reasons listed above, I find that the Appellant has not established that she faces a serious possibility of persecution in Nigeria and is therefore not a Convention refugee. Section 97 Analysis

The Appellant alleges that the RPD failed to conduct a section 97 analysis on the Appellant's claim. The RPD found that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellant would not be subjected to a risk to her life, or a risk of cruel and unusual punishment, or a danger of torture, should she be returned to Nigeria.

As the Appellant has not established that she is being sought after by the Chief in order to force her to marry him, or for any reason, nor has she established that her boyfriend is looking to force her or her baby to undergo FGM or otherwise, I agree with the RPD and find that the Appellant has not established that she is at risk in Nigeria.

For these reasons, I find that the Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that she faces a risk to her life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger of torture and is therefore not a person in need of protection under section 97.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
